tone_statements.citation: Sharma, D. D. (1988). A Descriptive Grammar of Kinnauri. Delhi: Mittal Publications. xvi+203 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Kinnauri neither, like English, is a stressed language, nor, like Chinese, a tonal one, since change in stress or pitch pattern on small units of an utterance does not bring about any significant change in the meaning of it, though at the syntactic level variation in pitch patterns may bring about change in the implied meaning of the sentence. [...] Usually in a polysyllabic word the initial syllable has a higher stress and the non-initial a higher pitch. Being non-phonemic these features have an arbitrary character and can occur in free variation within a given utterance, e.g. in /migspu/ 'eyebrow' the initial syllable may have a higher stress and in /syalic/ it may have a higher pitch, or prominence.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant initial, not in the strict set, word and phrase together domain) rests on Sharma 1988, a published reference grammar that we hold and whose deciding passage I confirmed verbatim (pp.45-46; plus the gemination remark p.~40 attributing gemination to 'higher stress on the preceding syllable'). The source itself calls stress non-phonemic, 'usually' initial and in free variation with non-initial pitch, so the non-strict dominant-initial coding with the existing word/phrase-lumping correction is the faithful reading; nothing found argues for a different position. sources.quote: 'Kinnauri has some pitches or stresses, but as can be seen below, there are only a few words that have pitch contrasts (tones are not accurate) [5 minimal pairs + a suffix pair] ... These examples show that Kinnauri has tone contrast in some cases. Kinnauri words are pronounced with a conventional pitch pattern. As for tones, more research is necessary.' No word-stress placement rule; flags marginal lexical pitch contrasts (Pangi dialect).
sources.venue: Link Languages and Archetypes in Tibeto-Burman

sources.citation: Takahashi, Yoshiharu. 2001. A descriptive study of Kinnauri (Pangi dialect): a preliminary report. In Y. Nagano & R. LaPolla (eds), New Research on Zhangzhung and Related Himalayan Languages (Senri Ethnological Reports 19), 97-119. Osaka: National Museum of Ethnology.
sources.quote: 'Kinnauri has some pitches or stresses, but there are only a few words which have pitch contrasts, as following (tones are not accurate): tu:m- [51] squeeze vs [11] swell; ran [53] horse vs [12] hill area; shan [54] small stone vs [12] throat. Suprasegmentals are to be further observed.' No statement on stress location.
sources.venue: New Research on Zhangzhung and Related Himalayan Languages
